entry.title: Barresi v Cross Yarra Partnerships [2026] VSC 666
entry.content:
The plaintiff sought judicial review of a second Wrongs Act Medical Panel determination that his whole person impairment did not meet the threshold, after an earlier panel had found that it did. The Court followed Citywide Service Solutions Pty Ltd v Rosata in permitting the later panel to determine the same medical question, and rejected the challenge based on s 28LZG(4). The catchwords record “Appeal dismissed”.

Key holding: An asserted misunderstanding by a Medical Panel of s 28LZG(4) will not constitute jurisdictional error unless the misunderstanding was material to the determination, in the sense that the decision could realistically have been different.

Consequently, in my opinion, the plaintiff has not established that the asserted misunderstanding by the second Panel of s 28LZG(4) was material to the decision that the second Panel made and therefore jurisdictional error has not been established.

entry.title: GWN25 by his Litigation Representative the Public Advocate v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1535
entry.content:
GWN25 sought judicial review of an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of his visa under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Minister conceded jurisdictional error in light of Minister for Immigration and Citizenship v DVRL, and the parties jointly proposed certiorari and mandamus. The Federal Court set aside the Tribunal decision and remitted the matter for redetermination, with costs.

Key holding: When assessing community risk under the relevant ministerial direction, the Tribunal must consider the different levels of risk depending on the visa status the applicant would hold, where that issue is advanced and supported by evidence.

The effect of the full court's ruling in DVRL is that the Tribunal was obliged, when considering "... the risk to the Australian community ..." for the purposes of cl 8.1(2) of the applicable ministerial direction, to consider not merely the risk that the applicant might pose if his permanent visa were restored but also the risk that he might pose as the holder of an ongoing bridging visa.

entry.title: Foong v Health Care Complaints Commission [2026] NSWCA 217
entry.content:
Dr Andrew Foong sought leave to appeal from NCAT’s refusal to recuse Principal Member Ainslie-Wallace AM ADCJ in disciplinary proceedings brought by the Health Care Complaints Commission. The alleged apprehended bias arose because the Principal Member had sat on a Medical Tribunal in 2010 with Dr Emery Kertesz, who was the Commission’s sole expert witness in the current proceedings. The Court of Appeal granted leave but dismissed the appeal.

Key holding: A prior tribunal association with an expert witness will not, without more, create a reasonable apprehension of bias where the only feared influence is a favourable view of that expert’s expertise, and the expert’s credibility and relevant expertise are not in issue.

Here, the only relevant possibility was that the Principal Member had, by reason of prior association, formed and retained an attitude that Dr Kertesz had the expertise to give evidence as a general practitioner in disciplinary proceedings brought by the Commission against another general practitioner. This attitude had no potential to have any effect in the present proceedings as Dr Kertesz's expertise as a general practitioner was accepted.

entry.title: Onyema v Commonwealth of Australia (as represented by the Australian Taxation Office) (extension of time, application for stay) [2026] FCA 1530
entry.content:
Kenneth Onyema sought judicial review of the ATO’s decision to terminate his APS employment for unauthorised access to taxation records. In this interlocutory judgment, the Federal Court held that he did not need an extension of time, refused a stay of the termination decision, granted leave to amend, and fixed the proper respondents.

Key holding: Under s 11(1)(c) of the ADJR Act, an application for review is “lodged” when it comes into the possession of the Registry or its staff, not when it is later accepted and filed, so receipt within the prescribed period satisfies the time limit.

An application for review will be "lodged" when it comes into the possession of a Registry or a staff of a Registry: EIW20 at [67], quoting Hong v Minister for Immigration and Multicultural Affairs [1998] FCA 341; (1998) 82 FCR 468 at 471 (the Court).

entry.title: Lye v Comcare [2026] FCA 1517
entry.content:
This was a Federal Court appeal from an Administrative Review Tribunal decision concerning weekly compensation under the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Act 1988 (Cth). The Tribunal had equated Mr Lye’s capacity to work full-time usual hours in administrative duties with an ability to earn his normal weekly earnings, reducing compensation to zero. The Court found legal error and, by consent, set aside the decision and remitted the matter for redetermination.

Key holding: Under s 19(2) of the SRC Act, the Tribunal must separately assess the amount per week the employee is able to earn in suitable employment and use that to determine the reduction to NWE; merely equating capacity for normal hours with NWE is legal error.

In its reasons at [40], the Tribunal failed to address the amount per week (if any) that the applicant was able to earn in suitable employment during the relevant periods (i.e., the fourth question). As a result of the above failure, the Tribunal failed properly to address the amount (if any) by which the applicant's NWE should be reduced in order to determine the amount of compensation that he is entitled to receive (i.e., the sixth question).

entry.title: Mohamedali v Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 1531
entry.content:
The Federal Court allowed a consent judicial review application concerning a decision by the Assistant Minister under s 501BA of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to cancel the applicant’s visa. The Assistant Minister conceded jurisdictional error because he failed to consider an updated psychologist’s report that was constructively before him and relevant to the applicant’s risk of reoffending. The Court made orders quashing the cancellation decision.

Key holding: A s 501BA decision is affected by jurisdictional error if the Minister fails to properly consider material constructively before him that is relevant to the risk the applicant poses to the Australian community and the national interest.

Accordingly, the Assistant Minister accepts that his decision was affected by jurisdictional error as a result of his failure to properly consider the risk the applicant posed to the Australian community.

entry.title: AQP23 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1521
entry.content:
AQP23 appealed from the Federal Circuit and Family Court, which had dismissed judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming cancellation of her protection visa under s 109 of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) for incorrect answers about citizenship. On appeal to the Federal Court, she argued the Tribunal’s hijab-related harm finding was legally unreasonable and that it failed to consider lesser “non-PV” harm. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal with costs.

Key holding: A tribunal is not required to expressly engage with claims about lesser forms of harm that the applicant has not clearly made.

It could scarcely be said that the Tribunal was required to expressly engage with claims about lesser forms of harm, including the "hijab sanction" and "non-PV harm", when the appellant never made claims clearly expressed in such terms

entry.title: Smith v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1520
entry.content:
Mr Smith, a New Zealand citizen, had his Class TY Subclass 444 visa cancelled under s 501(3A) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) after criminal convictions and imprisonment. A delegate refused to revoke the cancellation, and the Administrative Review Tribunal affirmed that refusal. On judicial review, the Federal Court found the Tribunal misconstrued Direction 110’s definition of “family violence” and set aside its decision.

Key holding: Conduct falling within an example of family violence in Direction 110 cl 4 is not automatically family violence; it must also have the effect of coercing or controlling a family member or causing that person to be fearful.

For example, behaviour which involves "intentionally damaging or destroying property" will not necessarily constitute family violence. It will only do so if that behaviour had the effect of coercing or controlling a member of the perpetrator's family, or causing the family member or members to be fearful.

entry.title: Gautama v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1519
entry.content:
The applicant sought judicial review of an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming the non-revocation of his cancelled Five-Year Resident Return (Class BB) (Subclass 155) visa under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). He argued the Tribunal erred by failing to apply the s 201 “10-year rule”, failing to consider mandatory considerations and misconstruing s 501CA(4)(b)(ii) as discretionary. The Federal Court dismissed the application.

Key holding: Section 201 of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), the “10-year rule”, has no application to mandatory visa cancellation under s 501(3A), because s 201 belongs to the separate deportation framework.

I accept the Minister's submissions. The Tribunal was correct in its conclusion that s 201 had no application to the matter before it.

entry.title: Papa v Commissioner of Police [2026] NSWSC 1263
entry.content:
The plaintiff sought judicial review of decisions revoking his Category AB firearms licence, including the original revocation and an internal review affirming it. The Supreme Court held only the internal review decision was operative and reviewable, found no failure to consider mandatory considerations or legal unreasonableness, and dismissed the summons.

Key holding: Where an original administrative decision is affirmed on internal review under s 53 of the ADR Act 1997 (NSW), only the review decision is legally operative and amenable to judicial review.

That conclusion, which was essentially argued by the defendant, means that, in the present circumstances, the second is the operative decision. It is only that decision which is amenable to judicial review.

entry.title: Younes v Younes (No 2) [2026] NSWSC 1261
entry.content:
Lolita Younes sought declaratory relief and specific performance concerning agreements relating to the subdivision/sale of the front block at 36 Page Street, Wentworthville. The substantive claim and Susie Younes’s cross-claim were dismissed by consent after subdivision and transfer to Lolita were completed. Stern J determined the reserved costs issue on the papers and made no order as to costs.

Key holding: Where proceedings are dismissed by consent without a merits determination, the court may make no order as to costs if it cannot conclude any party acted unreasonably or would have succeeded on the merits.

In these circumstances I am not satisfied that any one party has acted unreasonably in commencing or defending proceedings or that any one party would have been successful had the various claims been determined on their merits. Having regard to this, the appropriate order is that there be no order as to the costs of the proceedings

entry.title: Morton v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] HCA 38
entry.content:
The High Court dismissed Gary Gerard Morton's application for constitutional writs challenging a delegate's refusal of a Return (Residence) (Class BB) visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). Morton alleged the delegate failed to consider his claims about access to HIV, mental health and sobriety supports in Singapore and made legally unreasonable risk findings. The Court found no jurisdictional error, granted a short extension of time and dismissed the application with costs.

Key holding: A decision-maker is not required to give reasons by reference to every separate provision of Direction 110 or to repeat, in each relevant paragraph, the evaluation of information considered elsewhere.

Nothing in Direction 110 or s 501G(1) of the Migration Act requires a decision-maker to give reasons for their decision in a form which sets out the totality of the decision-maker's reasons by reference to each separate provision of Direction 110 including every piece of information evaluated and every finding of fact relevant to the decision-maker's assigning of weight to the specified matter which the provision requires the decision-maker to consider.

entry.title: Jaworski v Chartered Accountants Australia and New Zealand (No 2) [2026] NSWCA 213
entry.content:
Mr Jaworski sought to set aside or vary the Court of Appeal’s earlier leave judgment under UCPR r 36.16, and CA ANZ sought gross sum costs. The Court dismissed the reopening application and fixed costs at $30,000 for the leave/recusal application and $6,000 for CA ANZ’s notice of motion. The dispute concerned alleged errors, bias/prejudgment and costs in ongoing litigation involving CA ANZ.

Key holding: Under UCPR r 36.16, reopening requires some error in the court's reasoning due to misapprehension of fact or law that is not solely attributable to the applicant's neglect or default.

What is required to be established on an application under r 36.16 is some error in the court's reasoning because of a misapprehension of the facts or misapprehension of the relevant law; and that this misapprehension cannot be attributed solely to the neglect or default of the party seeking the rehearing.

entry.title: Lawrence, in the matter of Lawrence [2026] FCA 1507
entry.content:
Wayne James Lawrence applied under s 37AR(2) of the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 (Cth) for leave to institute an appeal from the primary judgment in Sammut v Lawrence [2025] FCA 1040, which made a vexatious proceedings order under s 37AO and dismissed his applications to set aside the fourth and fifth bankruptcy notices. Younan J refused leave, finding none of the proposed grounds of appeal reasonably arguable and the proposed appeal vexatious. The application was dismissed with costs, with lump-sum costs to be determined on the papers.

Key holding: On an application for leave under s 37AR of the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 (Cth), the applicant bears the onus of demonstrating that the proposed proceeding is not vexatious, which ordinarily requires that proposed grounds of appeal be reasonably arguable.

In accordance with s 37AT(4), it is for the applicant to demonstrate that the proposed appeal is not a vexatious proceeding, and with a view to that conclusion (although there may be other relevant factors), to demonstrate that any of the proposed grounds of appeal are reasonably arguable.

entry.title: BAH21 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1516
entry.content:
In BAH21 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1516, the applicant sought an extension of time to appeal a Federal Circuit and Family Court decision dismissing judicial review of an AAT decision on a protection visa. The applicant was offshore with no right to return and could not satisfy the in-Australia criterion for the visa, so the proposed appeal was futile. The Federal Court refused the extension and awarded costs.

Key holding: An extension of time will be refused where the proposed appeal is futile because the applicant is offshore and cannot satisfy the statutory requirement that they be in Australia to be granted a protection visa.

The Minister submitted that because the applicant is offshore and unable to re-enter Australia, she cannot be granted the protection visa, making the application for an extension of time and any appeal effectively futile. It is a relevant criterion for a protection visa that the applicant must be in Australia: clause 866.411 of Schedule 2 to the Migration Regulations 1994 (Cth).

entry.title: Pokharel v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1498
entry.content:
The Federal Court dismissed an application for review of a Federal Circuit and Family Court decision refusing an extension of time under s 477(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to challenge a student visa grant. The primary judge found a strong substantive case but refused the extension because of a 302-day delay and an unsatisfactory explanation. The Federal Court found no jurisdictional error in that refusal.

Key holding: Under s 477(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), an extension of time is not automatically required merely because the underlying judicial review case has strong merits; the court must be satisfied that the extension is necessary in the interests of the administration of justice.

That test does not require that an extension of time must always be granted where a primary judge has found merit in the underlying application for judicial review of a decision. Rather, the test is what is "necessary in the interests of the administration of justice", as her Honour recognised and applied at J[112], recited above.

entry.title: BPK17 v Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 1508
entry.content:
This was an appeal to the Federal Court from the Federal Circuit and Family Court (Division 2) dismissing judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Protection (Class XA) visa. The appellant did not appear and was outside Australia without any realistic prospect of return, making any appeal moot. The Court dismissed the appeal with costs under s 25(2B)(bb)(ii) of the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 (Cth) and r 36.75(1)(a)(i) of the Federal Court Rules 2011 (Cth).

Key holding: Where an appellant does not appear and the appeal is moot because no useful relief could be granted, the Court may treat the appeal as abandoned and dismiss it with costs.

In circumstances where the appellant did not appear and even if she had appeared the appeal would be moot, I am satisfied that the appellant has abandoned the appeal and it is appropriate to make an order that the appeal be dismissed with costs.

entry.title: Environment Centre (NT) Inc v Minister for the Environment and Water (No 2) [2026] FCA 1493
entry.content:

Key holding: Under r 26.12(7), the court asks whether good reason exists to depart from the position that a discontinuing party pay the other party’s costs.

Applying these principles, the question is whether good reason has been shown to depart from the position referred to in r 26.12(7), namely that the discontinuing party (the ECNT) should pay the costs of the other party (Top End).

entry.title: Morgan v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1489
entry.content:
Brenton Morgan sought judicial review of the Assistant Minister’s decision under s 501BA(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to set aside the Administrative Review Tribunal’s revocation of his visa cancellation and cancel his Class TY Subclass 444 visa. He alleged legal unreasonableness because the Assistant Minister relied on his new partner relationship being “not yet tested in the community” without seeking updated information after his parole.

Key holding: A failure to seek updated information will not make a s 501BA decision legally unreasonable where the inference drawn from the available dated material—such as giving limited weight to a new relationship not yet tested by community life—is reasonably open and logically supported.

It was not legally unreasonable to regard a relationship that had existed outside of the prison environment for no more than eight weeks as a relationship that "had yet to be tested in the community". In the context of the reasons, it was a finding supported by logical grounds.

entry.title: Williams v Companies Auditors Disciplinary Board [2026] FCAFC 136
entry.content:
The Full Court dismissed an appeal from the primary judge’s refusal of judicial review of the Companies Auditors Disciplinary Board’s decision to cancel Mr Williams’ registration as a company auditor. The Board found he failed adequately and properly to perform his duties as auditor under s 1292(1)(d)(i) of the Corporations Act 2001 (Cth), principally because he was Engagement Partner for the 2012 LM Audit. The appeal concerned whether that impermissibly imposed vicarious responsibility for work done by others.

Key holding: Under s 1292(1)(d)(i) of the Corporations Act, an audit Engagement Partner may be held responsible for the overall quality and sufficiency of the audit and audit opinion, irrespective of who performed particular tasks, as a leadership responsibility rather than vicarious liability.

The Engagement Partner's responsibility for the audit is not confined to work personally undertaken by the Engagement Partner. The intention is plain: to impose responsibility on the Engagement Partner for the audit overall irrespective of who conducted particular tasks in the course of the audit in recognition of the Engagement Partner's leadership role (at [50]-[53] of the primary Judge's Decision).

entry.title: Guo v Hu [2026] NSWDC 368
entry.content:
In Guo v Hu [2026] NSWDC 368, the plaintiff sought to set aside or restrict inspection of documents produced by the Department of Home Affairs under a subpoena issued by the defendant in a contractual dispute over share repurchase and a $150,000 investment. The District Court declined to set aside the subpoena entirely but, under UCPR r 33.9(3), limited access to migration documents capable of bearing on the pleaded issues, with a schedule to divide Access Granted and Access Refused documents. Costs were costs in the cause.

Key holding: Where subpoenaed documents have been produced but only some are apparently relevant, the court may refuse to set aside the subpoena and instead restrict inspection under UCPR r 33.9(3) to documents bearing on pleaded issues, refusing access to irrelevant personal material.

The Court's task under r 33.9 is not confined to a binary choice between complete access and no access. There is no reason why restricted access orders cannot properly be made where documents contain confidential or highly personal information and where only part of the material bears upon matters genuinely in dispute.

entry.title: JACOBS -v- HER HONOUR MAGISTRATE WARD [2026] WASC 435
entry.content:
Ms Jacobs, a public housing tenant, sought judicial review of a Magistrates Court decision dismissing her Residential Tenancies Act claims and finding no jurisdiction over her Australian Consumer Law claims. The Supreme Court found a reasonably arguable case and identified jurisdictional errors arising from denial of natural justice and misconstruction of RTA provisions. The decision was quashed in part and remitted to the Magistrates Court, differently constituted.

Key holding: On judicial review under s 36 MCA and s 26(2) RTA, an inferior court’s decision is affected by jurisdictional error only where it fails to exercise judicial power itself, including by misconceiving its statutory function or power, rather than merely making an error within jurisdiction.

These cases confirm that the relevant inquiry upon an application for judicial review of a decision of an inferior court is whether there has been a failure of the judicial officer to exercise judicial power itself or whether the judicial officer has merely made an error while exercising that judicial power. The former will generally constitute jurisdictional error; the latter will not.

entry.title: Mwambwa v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (No 2) [2026] FCA 1510
entry.content:
In Mwambwa v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (No 2) [2026] FCA 1510, Vincent Mwambwa sought an interlocutory injunction restraining the Minister from removing him from Australia pending his appeal concerning refusal of a bridging visa. The Federal Court found a serious but not strong case on appeal, but held the balance of convenience did not favour an injunction because a successful appeal was unlikely to preserve his right to remain.

Key holding: An interlocutory injunction pending appeal should be refused where, despite a serious case, the appeal is likely futile because it will not preserve the appellant's ability or right to remain in Australia, so the balance of convenience favours allowing the Minister to administer the Migration Act.

entry.content:
This was a costs-only decision after a preliminary discovery application under UCPR r 5.3 resolved informally. The plaintiffs sought costs alleging the first defendant capitulated; the first defendant sought its compliance costs under UCPR r 5.8. Campbell J refused the plaintiffs’ costs, refused the first defendant’s general legal costs, but awarded $12,500 gross sum for costs of compliance.

Key holding: For costs following resolution of a preliminary discovery application without a merits determination, UCPR r 5.8 creates no general presumption for or against a costs order; the court applies Lai Qin and the particular circumstances.

The effect of the absence of a rule is that there is no general presumption militating either in favour of or against the making of an order under UCPR r 5.8. I am guided by the authority of Lai Qin which was relied upon by both parties.
